prose:
Write an English explanation for a nontechnical project owner based on the incident report below. Explain what happened, what the evidence does and does not establish, and propose a fair next test. Use concrete numbers when available. Cover response latency, sustained throughput, memory, cache effects, and whether the proposed change is worth keeping. Do not invent measurements. Make the reasoning useful to someone deciding whether to adopt an optimization.

Incident report:

A small team is evaluating a local language model on a laptop with 48 GiB of shared CPU and GPU memory. The owner normally uses the laptop for development and wants useful answers without waiting for a remote service. The model files stay on the internal SSD. The experiment uses the same quantized model and the same helper model in every arm. It does not change the number of parameters or the stored precision. The helper proposes several tokens, and the main model verifies them. The user wants to know whether an improvement makes the first answer arrive sooner, makes the remaining answer arrive faster, or merely reduces bookkeeping.

The ordinary GPU scheduler prepares work for every expert even when the routing decisions send that expert no tokens. Some GPU jobs immediately return without performing a matrix multiplication. The proposed scheduler builds a work list from those same routing decisions and launches only the useful expert and token tile combinations, plus a small bounded number of surplus jobs. The work list needs an extra GPU kernel and an extra dependency barrier. Those costs belong in the candidate timing. A smaller count of launched jobs is a mechanism observation, not a measured speed improvement.

The initial screen uses two complete dependent model blocks. Each block includes gate and up projections, the activation function, the down projection, the expert combination, and the residual addition. Only the final residual is retained during timing. Inputs live in separate allocations. The original and candidate use identical weight bytes, input bytes, and selected expert IDs. The test repeats after changing the input and IDs, then restores the first data set to check that stale scratch has not survived. A counter records how often the candidate scheduler was encoded, and completed GPU graphs provide a separate execution check.

Three routing patterns matter. A uniform pattern spreads selected experts across the full expert set. A shared pattern sends every token to the same ten experts. A mixed pattern combines a few shared experts with a wider spread. Real model routing can differ from all three. One boundary fixture deliberately fills the work list to its proven capacity. Other fixtures exercise short prompts, long prompts, different ID strides, unsupported shapes, and higher input magnitude with the existing scaling path. Results from a synthetic route cannot automatically be described as a real model throughput gain.

The proposed adoption procedure begins with independent fresh process launches in the order original, candidate, candidate, original. Each workload receives an excluded warmup followed by repeated measurements. The observer records the raw output, the time to the first token, the whole reply time, generation tokens per second, and prompt tokens per second. The two original launches reveal control drift. A result smaller than that drift is inconclusive even if its sign is favorable. Outputs must match exactly for this scheduling-only experiment. A disagreement stops the comparison rather than becoming a speed win.

The memory monitor takes a baseline before launching the child process. Existing swap is reported separately. Any newly allocated swap stops the run and excludes it from the clean comparison. A fast SSD does not make swapped memory equivalent to resident GPU-accessible memory. Process RSS can double-count shared pages and omit some Metal allocations, so it is not a complete unified-memory accounting method. The team records native allocation receipts as well. It leaves unrelated active work alone and never restarts a stopped VM merely to finish a benchmark.

The team has previously tested three other changes. One removed unnecessary attention ranking but produced effectively unchanged reply speed. Another cached token-to-text conversion and reduced service calls without a reliable end-to-end benefit. A third shared routing setup between adjacent projections and saved less than one percent in complete component blocks. The team parked those mechanisms and recorded the conditions under which a revisit would be justified. Their small percentages must not be added together, because they came from separate mechanisms and comparisons.

The current question is whether a work list saves enough complete processing time to justify a full model trial. If the screen passes, the model test should include practical English tasks with substantial context, because the scheduler mainly affects prompt processing. A short instruction with a long generated answer may hide the benefit. It would also be misleading to promise higher single-token generation throughput when that path never enters the new scheduler. A successful narrow latency improvement can still be useful, provided the report names the workload and the metric.

Explain how you would make the final decision, including what you would report if the work list is correct but the extra kernel erases its savings. End with a prioritized next action justified by the evidence, not an optimistic estimate.
